teaching.task: # HMS Year 12 V04 (Health in an Australian and global context): Australia among OECD countries. Where does Australia rank on health among wealthy countries, and why do some countries do better? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Whether a country's health is good is always a comparison. Compare Australia with a poor country, and you mostly learn about wealth. So we compare with the OECD, a group of mostly high-income countries that collect health data on agreed definitions. That holds wealth roughly steady, so the differences left point at choices: how the system is designed, what's spent on prevention, what's regulated. The most useful indicator is avoidable mortality: deaths that prevention or timely care could have stopped, because it shows what a system can influence. And three cautions. Rankings jump around, because many countries sit very close together. A national average can hide big gaps. And countries count differently. A difference in the data can be a difference in the counting. So where does Australia sit? Think groups, not rank numbers, because rank numbers move. Australia is in the leading group for life expectancy, for males and females. It does better than average on avoidable deaths. Its daily smoking rate is among the lowest, and its cancer survival among the better. But it's average or weaker on others. Overweight and obesity are above average, and have risen for decades. Alcohol use sits around average or above. And, as in most OECD countries, only a small share of spending goes to prevention. Out-of-pocket costs, what patients pay themselves, are higher than in several similar countries, and heaviest for dental care. And there are big gaps inside the country. Put both columns together: healthy on average, and unevenly so. Why? Sort explanations into three families. System: universal coverage through Medicare means cost is less often a barrier to seeing a GP, strong general practice catches problems early, and subsidised medicines keep long-term treatment affordable. Behaviour and policy: decades of tobacco control, with ad bans, taxes, plain packaging and smoke-free places, produced the low smoking rate, and fewer heart and cancer deaths follow. Population and environment: a younger population than many European and East Asian countries, and many migrants who arrive healthy. Now match the family to the indicator. Obesity, which raises heart disease and diabetes risk, isn't mainly a system failure. It comes from food environments, marketing and car-dependent suburbs, which is why clinics alone haven't shifted it. And high out-of-pocket costs are a system design outcome. They show up as delayed dental care, not delayed GP visits.

scenes.teachingReason: Whether a country's health is good is always a comparison. Compare Australia with a poor country, and you mostly learn about wealth. So we compare with the OECD, a group of mostly high-income countries that collect health data on agreed definitions. The most useful indicator is avoidable mortality: deaths that prevention or timely care could have stopped, because it shows what a system can influence. And three cautions. Rankings jump around, because many countries sit very close together. A national average can hide big gaps. And countries count differently. A difference in the data can be a difference in the counting.

scenes.teachingReason: Why? Sort explanations into three families. System: universal coverage through Medicare means cost is less often a barrier to seeing a GP, strong general practice catches problems early, and subsidised medicines keep long-term treatment affordable. Behaviour and policy: decades of tobacco control, with ad bans, taxes, plain packaging and smoke-free places, produced the low smoking rate, and fewer heart and cancer deaths follow. Population and environment: a younger population than many European and East Asian countries, and many migrants who arrive healthy. Now match the family to the indicator. Obesity, which raises heart disease and diabetes risk, isn't mainly a system failure. It comes from food environments, marketing and car-dependent suburbs, which is why clinics alone haven't shifted it. And high out-of-pocket costs are a system design outcome. They show up as delayed dental care, not delayed GP visits.

scenes.teachingReason: And why do some countries rank above or below us? Four variables explain most of the spread. One, whether coverage is universal. Where many people face cost as a barrier, avoidable deaths stay high, however advanced the hospitals. That answers the puzzle: the spending is real, but it isn't reaching everyone. Other answers could be an older population, or different counting. Two, how much goes to primary care and prevention, which act earlier in a disease. Three, income inequality and social spending, because health is made largely outside the health system. Four, long-standing patterns of diet, smoking and drinking, and the policies that shape them. And one idea explains many paradoxes: today's deaths reflect yesterday's exposures. A country that cut smoking thirty years ago is collecting the benefit now.

scenes.teachingReason: The last question is what we can learn and apply here. That needs a transfer test. Don't ask what another country does. Ask what makes it work, and whether that thing exists here. Step one, name the mechanism. Step two, check it against Australia: how spread out we are, our tax base, where our health workers live, and what's already covered. If the mechanism exists here, the policy transfers, with adaptations. If it doesn't, only the principle transfers, and you find a local way to carry it. So what passes? Sustained regulation, which worked for tobacco, applied to food marketing. Shifting spending toward prevention and primary care. And reporting by group, not just nationally. What fails? Anything that relies on dense cities, or on health workers spread evenly.
